claim: ZFP36 protein levels peak approximately 4 hours post-activation in primary mouse CD4+ T cells.
source: Protein levels peaked ~4 hr post-activation and tapered gradually through 72 hr, and were re-induced by re-stimulation 3 days post-activation (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1A demonstrating time course of ZFP36 expression

claim: ZFP36 expression depends on both TCR stimulation and co-stimulation in CD4+ T cells.
source: ZFP36 expression depended on both TCR stimulation, provided by anti-CD3, and co-stimulation, provided by co-cultured dendritic cells (DCs) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis testing different stimulation conditions

claim: A similar pattern of transient ZFP36 induction occurs in activated CD8+ T cells.
source: A similar pattern of transient ZFP36 induction occurred in activated CD8 +T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in supplementary figure

claim: ZFP36 and ZFP36L1 are induced by T-cell activation.
source: Western analysis showed that both ZFP36 and ZFP36L1 were induced by T-cell activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis with paralog-specific antibodies

claim: ZFP36L2 was not detected under any conditions examined in T cells.
source: ZFP36L2, expected to run at ~62 kD, was not detected under any conditions examined.
evidence: Based on Western blot analysis

claim: Activated Zfp36 KO T cells have partial loss (~50%) of pan ZFP36 expression.
source: Analysis of Zfp36 KO T cell lysates with pan ZFP36 antisera showed ~50% reduced signal compared to WT. We conclude that the residual signal is likely due to persistent expression of ZFP36L1, which is highly homologous and of similar size to ZFP36.
evidence: Based on Western blot quantification comparing WT and KO cells

claim: Zfp36 and Zfp36l1 mRNAs are robustly present in naïve CD4+ T cells despite absence of detectable protein.
source: Interestingly, Zfp36 (RPKM = 22.5) and Zfp36l1 (RPKM = 8.2) mRNAs are robustly present in RNAseq data from naïve CD4 +T cells, despite an absence of detectable protein by western blotting.
evidence: Based on RNAseq data and Western blot analysis

claim: Post-transcriptional mechanisms regulate expression of ZFP36 paralogs in T cells.
source: These observations indicate that post-transcriptional mechanisms regulate expression of ZFP36 paralogs in T cells.
evidence: Inferred from presence of mRNA without detectable protein

claim: ZFP36/L1 sites show a preponderance of 3'-UTR binding (>75%).
source: Globally, ZFP36/L1 sites confirmed a preponderance of 3'-UTR binding (>75%), and showed substantial binding in coding sequence (CDS;~6.5%) and introns (5.4%) (Figure 1F).
evidence: Based on annotation of HITS-CLIP binding sites

claim: ZFP36 and ZFP36L1 have similar binding profiles in vivo.
source: Sites in WT and Zfp36 KO cells showed very similar enriched motifs and transcript localizations, indicating that ZFP36 and ZFP36L1 have similar binding profiles in vivo (Figure 1E–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Comparison of HITS-CLIP data from WT and Zfp36 KO cells

claim: Majorities of robust sites (53%) and target mRNAs (66%) identified in WT cells were found independently in Zfp36 KO cells.
source: Majorities of robust sites (53%) and target mRNAs (66%) identified in WT cells were found independently in Zfp36 KO cells, and site overlap was far greater (>90%) for peaks of increasing magnitude (Figure 1G).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of HITS-CLIP sites between WT and KO

claim: ZFP36 binding in 3'UTRs is most concentrated in the vicinity of expected polyA sites, approximately 50 nucleotides before transcript ends.
source: Accordingly, ZFP36 binding in 3'UTRs was most concentrated in the vicinity of expected polyA sites,~50 nucleotides before transcript ends (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Based on coverage map analysis of HITS-CLIP data

claim: At least a subset of CDS binding by ZFP36 occurs prior to pre-mRNA splicing in the nucleus.
source: Cross-link-induced truncations (CITS) clarified that CDS peaks are centered within coding exons, but supporting CLIP reads often spanned the exon-intron boundary. Thus, at least a subset of CDS binding by ZFP36 occurs prior to pre-mRNA splicing in the nucleus.
evidence: Based on analysis of CLIP reads spanning exon-intron boundaries

claim: ZFP36 binding in 3'UTR and CDS correlates with subtle but highly significant shifts toward greater mRNA abundance in Zfp36 KO cells.
source: The second main effect emerged from a global analysis, which showed ZFP36 binding in 3'UTR (p=4.44×10−16; Kolmogorov-Smirnoff [KS]) and CDS (p=5.33×10−11) correlated to subtle but highly significant shifts toward greater mRNA abundance in Zfp36 KO cells, relative to mRNAs with no binding sites (Figure 1H).
evidence: RNAseq analysis comparing WT and Zfp36 KO cells with statistical testing

claim: mRNAs with ZFP36 binding exclusively in introns do not show correlation with altered RNA abundance.
source: This correlation was not observed for mRNAs with binding exclusively in introns, and we did not find evidence in these data that ZFP36/L1 binding correlated with altered usage of proximal splice or polyA sites (not shown).
evidence: Based on RNAseq analysis

claim: mRNAs containing the top 20% most robust 3'UTR ZFP36 binding sites show no significant effect on RNA abundance in Zfp36 KO cells.
source: For 3'UTR binding, ZFP36 targets overall showed a significant shift in abundance, but mRNAs containing the top 20% most robust sites (ranked by peak height [PH], see Materials and methods) showed no significant effect. Thus, a higher degree of binding correlated with less effect on RNA abundance in the absence of ZFP36 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Stratified analysis of RNAseq data by CLIP binding magnitude

claim: CD69, BCL2, TNF, and IFNG show significantly increased protein levels in Zfp36 KO versus WT T cells 4 hours after activation.
source: Activation marker CD69, apoptosis regulator BCL2, and effector cytokines TNF and IFNG showed significantly increased protein levels in Zfp36 KO versus WT T cells 4 hr after activation (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Flow cytometry measurements of protein levels

claim: Only Bcl2 showed increased mRNA abundance among CD69, TNF, IFNG, and BCL2 targets.
source: Of these, only Bcl2 showed increased mRNA abundance.
evidence: Based on RNAseq data

claim: Tnf, Ifng, and Cd69 are among the top 20% of ZFP36 targets as defined by CLIP binding magnitude.
source: Tnf, Ifng, and Cd69 were all among the top 20% of targets as defined by CLIP binding magnitude (PH), thus supporting the trend in our global analyses that some highly robust binding targets show little regulation at the level of mRNA abundance in this context.
evidence: Based on HITS-CLIP peak height analysis

claim: ZFP36 strongly represses protein expression for Cd69, Tnf, and Ifng WT-UTR reporters in 293 cells.
source: In 293 cells, ZFP36 strongly repressed protein expression for all three WT-UTR reporters, while showing weaker (Tnf and Ifng) or no (Cd69) repression of mRNA levels.
evidence: Reporter assay data in transfected 293 cells

claim: Repression of WT-UTR constructs by ZFP36 is consistently greater than for Δ-UTR variants.
source: However, repression of WT-UTR constructs was consistently greater than for Δ-UTR variants, demonstrating specific ZFP36 repression of the defined binding sites.
evidence: Comparison of reporter assays with intact vs deleted binding sites

claim: ZFP36 target mRNAs show increased ribosome association in Zfp36 KO cells.
source: Globally, there was a subtle but significant shift toward greater ribosome association in Zfp36 KO cells for mRNAs bound by ZFP36 in 3'UTR (p=1.04×10−11; KS) or CDS (p=1.58×10−11), relative to mRNAs with no ZFP36 binding (Figure 3B).
evidence: Ribosome profiling data with statistical analysis

claim: mRNAs with ZFP36 binding in CDS show a significantly larger shift in ribosome association than those with 3'UTR binding.
source: These shifts mirror those for global RNA abundance, with two notable exceptions. First, mRNAs with ZFP36 binding in CDS showed a significantly larger shift in ribosome association than those with 3'UTR binding (Figure 3B).
evidence: Comparison of ribosome profiling data for different binding site locations

claim: ZFP36 3'UTR and CDS binding targets are strongly enriched for increased translation efficiency in Zfp36 KO cells.
source: ZFP36 3'UTR and, more significantly, CDS binding targets were strongly enriched for increased TE in Zfp36 KO cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: GSEA analysis of translation efficiency changes

claim: Normalized ribosome coverage on Tnf and Ifng is significantly higher in Zfp36 KO cells than WT despite no detectable difference in overall mRNA abundance.
source: As a striking confirmation of these results, normalized ribosome coverage on robust 3'UTR targets Tnf and Ifng was significantly higher in Zfp36 KO cells than WT (Figure 3D), despite no detectable difference in overall mRNA abundance (Figure 2A).
evidence: Ribosome profiling and RNAseq data for specific targets

claim: Ribosome coverage averaged across all mRNAs is not appreciably different between KO and WT cells.
source: Crucially, ribosome coverage averaged across all mRNAs was not appreciably different between KO and WT cells, indicating specific effects on ZFP36 targets (Figure 3E).
evidence: Global ribosome profiling analysis

claim: ZFP36 prevents association of mRNAs with ribosomes but does not impact elongation.
source: Notably, the pattern of ribosome association along these and other transcripts is remarkably consistent between WT and Zfp36 KO cells, but with altered magnitude. Mechanistically, this observation indicates that ZFP36 prevents association of mRNAs with ribosomes, but does not impact elongation.
evidence: Analysis of ribosome profiling read distribution patterns

claim: ZFP36 targets are enriched for mRNAs that are rapidly induced after T-cell activation.
source: ZFP36 targets were enriched for mRNAs, like its own, that were rapidly induced after T-cell activation, and targets were depleted among mRNAs with stable expression or delayed induction (Figure 4A).
evidence: Analysis of ZFP36 target distribution in published T-cell activation time course data

claim: Naïve Zfp36 KO CD4+ T cells show greater proliferation than WT from 16 to 24 hours post-activation.
source: In thymidine incorporation assays, naïve Zfp36 KO CD4 +T cells showed greater proliferation than WT from 16 to 24 hr post-activation (Figure 4C).
evidence: Thymidine incorporation assay data

claim: Increased proliferation in Zfp36 KO cells reflects decreased apoptosis and increased numbers of proliferating cells.
source: This increase reflected decreased apoptosis (Figure 4D) and increased numbers of proliferating cells (Figure 4E) in KO versus WT cultures.
evidence: Flow cytometry measurements of apoptosis and proliferation markers

claim: Zfp36 KO T cells proliferate more than WT both in the presence of excess recombinant IL-2 or neutralizing anti-IL-2 antibody.
source: Zfp36 KO T cells proliferated more than WT both in the presence of excess recombinant IL-2 or neutralizing anti-IL-2 antibody, as well as in different Th polarizing conditions, indicating the effect is not solely IL-2-dependent (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: Proliferation assays under various cytokine conditions

claim: BG2 transgenic Zfp36 KO cells show greater proliferation than WT across a broad titration of cognate peptide.
source: BG2 transgenic Zfp36 KO cells showed greater proliferation than WT across a broad titration of cognate peptide, but not irrelevant peptide (Figure 4F).
evidence: Proliferation assays with TCR transgenic cells and peptide titration

claim: Zfp36 KO T cells show greater proliferation than WT in response to allogeneic DCs.
source: Second, Zfp36 KO T cells also showed greater proliferation than WT in response to allogeneic DCs (Figure 4G).
evidence: Allogeneic response assay data

claim: Zfp36 KO cells show enhanced induction of CD69 and CD25 over the first 24 hours post-activation.
source: Analysis of canonical T-cell activation markers revealed enhanced induction of CD69 and CD25 in Zfp36 KO versus WT cells over the first 24 hr post-activation (Figure 4H).
evidence: Flow cytometry measurements of activation markers

claim: A greater proportion of Zfp36 KO cells transition from naïve to effector surface phenotype at 40 hours post-activation compared to WT.
source: At 40 hr post-activation, a greater proportion of Zfp36 KO versus WT had transitioned from a naïve to effector surface phenotype (Figure 4I).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis of naïve and effector markers

claim: ZFP36 regulation of T-cell activation is cell-intrinsic.
source: Naïve Zfp36 KO T cells sorted from chimeras showed greater proliferation than WT 24 hr post-activation, indicating cell-intrinsic effects (Figure 5B).
evidence: Proliferation assays with cells sorted from mixed bone marrow chimeras

claim: WT cells can exert a restraining effect on Zfp36 KO cells.
source: Interestingly, the reduced proliferation of Zfp36 KO cells in mixed (Figure 5B, right panel) versus separate (left panel) cultures indicate that WT cells can exert a restraining effect on KO cells.
evidence: Comparison of proliferation in separate vs mixed cultures

claim: Many transcripts show highly divergent expression in Zfp36 KO versus WT T cells 3 days after activation.
source: First, in contrast to subtle effects observed at the 4 hr time point, many transcripts showed highly divergent expression in Zfp36 KO versus WT T cells 3 days after activation (Figure 6A).
evidence: RNAseq analysis at 72 hours post-activation

claim: Differences in gene expression at 72 hours post-activation are not correlated to ZFP36 HITS-CLIP binding.
source: However, these differences were not correlated to ZFP36 HITS-CLIP binding at 72 hr (Figure 6B). Thus, the absence of ZFP36 in the early phases of T -cell activation can lead to significant secondary effects downstream.
evidence: Comparison of RNAseq and HITS-CLIP data at 72 hours

claim: Enhanced IFN-γ production in Zfp36 KO cells at early time points gives way to comparable production by day three and reduced production by day 5.
source: Consistent with a late activated and exhausted phenotype in Zfp36 KO cells, the enhanced production of IFN-γ at early time points (Figures 2A and 3D) gave way to comparable production by day three and reduced production by day 5 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Intracellular cytokine staining at multiple time points

claim: There is higher accumulation of IFN-γ and TNF-α in Zfp36 KO culture supernatants 72 hours post-activation.
source: The net result, reflecting both dysregulated cytokine production and more rapid culture expansion (Figures 4 and 5), is a higher accumulation of IFN-γ and TNF-αin Zfp36 KO culture supernatants 72 hr post-activation (Figure 6E).
evidence: ELISA measurements of cytokines in culture supernatants

claim: Elevated expression of PD-1 and ICOS at late time points in Zfp36 KO cells is observed in Th1 but not Th0 conditions.
source: We examined co-inhibitory and co-stimulatory checkpoint proteins that are linked to T cell exhaustion, and found elevated expression of PD-1 and ICOS at late time points in Zfp36 KO cells, and more rapid peaking of LAG-3 (Figure 6F). Interestingly, these effects were observed in Th1 but not Th0 conditions, suggesting a dependence on Th1 cytokines.
evidence: Flow cytometry measurements under different polarizing conditions

claim: Differential expression of PD-1, ICOS, and LAG-3 in Zfp36 KO cells is T cell-intrinsic but driven by secreted factors.
source: To test this dependence, and to examine whether elevated receptor expression was T cell-intrinsic, we analyzed cells derived from mixed BM chimeras. This analysis confirmed differential, T cell-intrinsic expression of these receptors (Figure 6G). However, re-mixing WT and KO cells ex vivo neutralized these differences, indicating they are driven by secreted factors.
evidence: Analysis of cells from mixed bone marrow chimeras with re-mixing experiments

claim: Recombinant IFN-γ promotes ICOS but not PD-1 upregulation in WT Th1 cells.
source: We tested whether recombinant IFN-γ, supplemented at levels measured in KO cultures, could cause elevated receptor expression in WT Th1 cells, and found it promoted ICOS but not PD-1 upregulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Experiments with recombinant cytokine supplementation

claim: Naïve Zfp36 KO mice have normal T cell levels in peripheral blood and no defects in thymocyte development.
source: We first determined that naïve Zfp36 KO mice had normal T cell levels in peripheral blood and no defects in thymocyte development (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis of blood and thymus

claim: Total splenocytes, including T cells, are slightly reduced in Zfp36 KO versus WT mice.
source: Total splenocytes, including T cells, were slightly reduced in Zfp36 KO versus WT mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), but proportions of total CD4 + and CD8+T cells were normal (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis of spleen

claim: More CD4+ and CD8+ T cells produce IFN-γ in KO versus WT splenocytes at steady state.
source: More CD4 + and CD8+T cells produced IFN-γin KO versus WT splenocytes, but levels of IL-4 and IL17A production were comparable (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H). Therefore, greater numbers of Th1 cells are present at steady state in Zfp36 KO mice.
evidence: Intracellular cytokine staining of ex vivo stimulated splenocytes

claim: Differentiation of Th1 and Th17 subsets ex vivo is indistinguishable in WT and Zfp36 KO cells.
source: To examine whether loss of ZFP36 causes an intrinsic disposition to the Th1 fate, skewing of sorted, naïve CD4 +T cells was examined. These analyses showed indistinguishable differentiation of Th1 and Th17 subsets ex vivo in WT and Zfp36 KO cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: In vitro T helper cell differentiation assays

claim: Accelerated expansion and recession of virus-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cells occurs in Zfp36 KO versus WT mice during LCMV infection.
source: Using MHC-tetramers, we observed accelerated expansion and recession of virus-specific CD4+ (Figure 7A) and CD8+ (Figure 7B) T cells in Zfp36 KO versus WT mice in peripheral blood.
evidence: MHC-tetramer staining of blood samples during LCMV infection time course

claim: Virus-specific T cells in Zfp36 KO mice show earlier expansion and more rapid upregulation of CD69 at early time points post-infection.
source: This result was confirmed in independent experiments focused on early time points post-infection (p.i.), where virus-specific T cells in Zfp36 KO mice showed earlier expansion and more rapid upregulation of CD69 (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: MHC-tetramer and CD69 staining at early infection time points

claim: Levels of virus-specific T cells are greater in Zfp36 KO animals 6 days post-infection but marginally lower by day 10.
source: Enumeration of virus-specific T cells in spleen mirrored dynamics in blood; levels were greater in Zfp36 KO animals 6 days p.i., but marginally lower by day 10, consistent with more rapid expansion and resolution (Figure 7E–F).
evidence: MHC-tetramer staining of spleen samples at multiple time points

claim: Levels of memory T cells day 40 post-infection are similar in Zfp36 KO and WT mice.
source: Levels of memory T cells day 40 p.i. were similar in Zfp36 KO and WT mice.
evidence: MHC-tetramer staining at late time point

claim: Zfp36 KO CD4+ and CD8+ T cells have higher rates of IFN-γ and TNF-α production 6 days post-infection.
source: Stimulation with LCMV peptides ex vivo revealed higher rates of IFN-γ and TNF-αproduction in Zfp36 KO versus WT CD4+ (Figure 7G) and CD8 +T cells 6 days p.i. (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Intracellular cytokine staining after peptide stimulation

claim: Levels of IFN-γ and TNF-α protein are significantly greater in CD4+ Zfp36 KO cytokine-producing cells versus WT.
source: However, levels of IFN-γand TNF-α protein were significantly greater in CD4 +Zfp36 KO cytokine-producing cells versus WT (Figure 7H), and TNF-α levels were also higher for CD8 +cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Mean fluorescence intensity measurements from intracellular cytokine staining

claim: Bifunctional IFN-γ+TNF-α+ T cells are more frequent in Zfp36 KO mice even when normalized to frequencies of tetramer+ cells.
source: In addition, 'bifunctional' IFN-γ+TNF-α+T cells were more frequent in Zfp36 KO mice, even when normalized to frequencies of tetramer +cells (Figure 7I and Figure 7—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis of dual cytokine-producing cells

claim: LCMV genomic RNA in spleen is approximately 10-fold lower day 6 post-infection in Zfp36 KO versus WT animals.
source: Strikingly, LCMV genomic RNA in spleen was ~10 fold lower day 6 p.i. in Zfp36 KO versus WT animals, consistent with more rapid clearance of LCMV infection (Figure 7J).
evidence: RT-qPCR measurement of viral RNA in spleen

claim: Viral load correlates inversely with levels of tetramer+ CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in both Zfp36 KO and WT mice.
source: Viral load correlated inversely with levels of tetramer +CD4+ and CD8+T cells in both Zfp36 KO and WT mice, consistent with the established role of T cell response in LCMV clearance (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Correlation analysis of viral load and T cell levels

claim: In mixed bone marrow chimeras, the kinetics of WT and Zfp36 KO T cell response to LCMV infection are indistinguishable.
source: Ten weeks after re-constitution, pre-infection baseline measurements showed a significantly greater expansion of Zfp36 KO T cells versus WT in blood (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B). However, the kinetics of WT and KO T cell response in these animals upon LCMV infection were indistinguishable (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C–D). Therefore, in a mixed environment in vivo, Zfp36 KO and WT T cells show similar kinetics upon viral challenge.
evidence: MHC-tetramer analysis in mixed bone marrow chimeras during LCMV infection

claim: Maximum T cell expansion in mixed chimeras was observed 7-8 days post-infection, which is intermediate to the maxima observed in Zfp36 KO (6 days) and WT (10 days) mice.
source: Notably, maximum T cell expansion was observed in mixed chimeras 7–8 days p.i., which was intermediate to the maxima observed in Zfp36 KO (6 days) and WT (10 days) mice.
evidence: Comparison of T cell expansion kinetics across different experimental conditions

claim: ZFP36 and ZFP36L1 expression are rapidly induced upon T-cell activation and gradually recede thereafter.
source: ZFP36 and ZFP36L1 expression are rapidly induced upon T-cell activation, and gradually recede thereafter.
evidence: Based on Western blot time course data

claim: Post-transcriptional mechanisms regulate expression of ZFP36 paralogs in T cells.
source: While transcriptional induction has been previously established, our detection of Zfp36 and Zfp36l1 mRNAs in naïve T cells, in the absence of detectable protein, indicates post-transcriptional regulation of their mRNAs in T cells.
evidence: Comparison of RNAseq and Western blot data

claim: Paralog auto- and cross-regulation of ZFP36 family members are likely in T cells.
source: Moreover, paralog auto- and cross-regulation are likely, as Zfp36 and Zfp36l1 mRNA 3'UTRs possess robust HITS-CLIP binding sites.
evidence: Presence of ZFP36 binding sites in ZFP36 paralog 3'UTRs from HITS-CLIP data

claim: ZFP36 attenuates T-cell activation by suppressing the abundance and translation of its mRNA targets.
source: Definitive determination of ZFP36 targets in T cells by HITS-CLIP, coupled with transcriptome and ribosome profiling studies, revealed that ZFP36 attenuates T-cell activation by suppressing the abundance and translation of its mRNA targets.
evidence: Integration of HITS-CLIP, RNAseq, and ribosome profiling data

claim: Different degrees of ZFP36 association in vivo may elicit distinct functional outcomes.
source: It is possible that different degrees of ZFP36 association in vivo elicit distinct functional outcomes, through differential RNP localization or downstream effector recruitment.
evidence: Based on observation of non-uniform effects stratified by binding magnitude

claim: ZFP36 CLIP shows a broad MW range of ZFP36-RNA complexes with distinct biochemical properties including stability to heat, detergent, and high salt.
source: Notably, ZPF36 CLIP showed a broad MW range of ZFP36-RNA complexes with distinct biochemical properties including stability to heat, detergent, and high salt.
evidence: Based on CLIP autoradiogram analysis

claim: Some ZFP36 CLIP reads in CDS sites span exon-intron boundaries, indicating these associations can form prior to pre-mRNA splicing in the nucleus.
source: Intriguingly, some ZFP36 CLIP reads in CDS sites spanned exon-intron boundaries, indicating these associations can form prior to pre-mRNA splicing in the nucleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Analysis of CLIP read alignment patterns

claim: The identification of AREs in the CDS and the possibility of resulting translation control pre-programmed in the nucleus point to novel, unexplored regulatory strategies.
source: The identification of AREs in the CDS and the possibility of resulting translation control pre-programmed in the nucleus point to novel, unexplored regulatory strategies.
evidence: Based on discovery of CDS binding sites and their properties

claim: The similarity of RNA-binding maps covering both ZFP36 and ZFP36L1 supports redundancy of ZFP36 paralogs.
source: The similarity of RNA-binding maps covering both ZFP36 and ZFP36L1 (WT cells) or ZFP36L1 alone (Zfp36 KO cells) supports redundancy of ZFP36 paralogs, a likely source of robustness in immune regulation.
evidence: Comparison of HITS-CLIP data from WT and Zfp36 KO cells

claim: Zfp36 KO cells are likely a partial loss-of-function due to robust ZFP36L1 expression.
source: Zfp36 KO cells are thus likely a partial loss-of-function due to robust ZFP36L1 expression, a notion consistent with the relatively subtle regulatory effects on RNA abundance and translation.
evidence: Based on Western blot and CLIP data showing persistent ZFP36L1 expression in KO cells

claim: Loss of Zfp36 leads to accelerated activation of mature T cells but not uncontrolled proliferation or impaired development.
source: Phenotypically, loss of Zfp36 led to accelerated activation of mature T cells, but not uncontrolled proliferation or impaired development, which may again may reflect a partial loss of pan ZFP36 activity.
evidence: Based on functional assays and developmental analysis

claim: Total paralog dosage is critical for ZFP36 family function in T cells.
source: Indeed, a prior study reported no effects when Zfp36l1 was deleted in T cells, but drastic dysregulation of thymocyte proliferation upon loss of both Zfp36l1 and Zfp36l2 (Hodson et al., 2010). These studies indicate total paralog dosage is critical, but also suggest the importance of the specific balance of ZFP36 paralogs in a defined context.
evidence: Comparison with published studies of paralog deletions

claim: The phenotype of Zfp36 KO T cells is novel and distinct, leading not to uncontrolled proliferation but to accelerated effector response and resolution.
source: However, the phenotype of Zfp36 KO T cells is novel and distinct, leading not to uncontrolled proliferation, but to accelerated effector response and resolution.
evidence: Summary of functional characterization data

claim: The combined picture of genomic and functional data shows many functionally diverse targets contributing to a multifaceted, finely tuned response.
source: More broadly, the combined picture of our genomic and functional data are one of many functionally diverse targets contributing to a multifaceted, finely tuned response, which is a hallmark of post-transcriptional regulatory control.
evidence: Integration of HITS-CLIP, functional assays, and GO analysis

claim: Secondary effects of ZFP36 loss predominate as T cell expansion and differentiation progress 3 days post-activation.
source: Notably, and in contrast to analyses early post-activation, changes in RNA abundance 3 days post-activation were not correlated to direct ZFP36 binding. Therefore, secondary effects of ZFP36 loss pre-dominate as T cell expansion and differentiation progress in these settings.
evidence: Comparison of RNAseq and HITS-CLIP data at 72 hours

claim: A dysregulated Th1 secretion profile including but not limited to elevated IFN-γ can push T cells to a state resembling exhaustion in vitro.
source: Notably, altered expression of co-inhibitory and –stimulatory receptors in Zfp36 KO cells was specific to Th1 cells (Figure 6F), and mixing experiments confirmed dependence on secreted factors (Figure 6G; Figure 6—figure supplement 2B). Thus, a dysregulated Th1 secretion profile including but not limited to elevated IFN-γ can push T cells to a state resembling exhaustion in vitro.
evidence: Analysis of receptor expression under different conditions and with cytokine supplementation

claim: Subtle, but direct, regulation of a broad range of targets early after T-cell activation by ZFP36 can have striking downstream consequences in a rapidly expanding cell population.
source: More broadly, these results highlight the crucial point that subtle, but direct, regulation of a broad range of targets early after T-cell activation by ZFP36 can have striking downstream consequences in a rapidly expanding cell population.
evidence: Integration of early and late time point analyses

claim: The accelerated anti-viral T cell response in Zfp36 KO mice may involve immune cell types in addition to T cells.
source: In mixed BM chimeras, the response kinetics of WT and Zfp36 KO T cells to LCMV infection were indistinguishable. This result raises the possibility that other cell types and pathways, such as antigen presenting cells, antibody response, or innate immune regulators, could contribute to the accelerated anti-viral T cell response in Zfp36 KO mice.
evidence: Based on mixed bone marrow chimera experiments

claim: The observation of enhanced LCMV clearance is likely T cell-dependent.
source: Regardless of the initiating mechanism, the observation of enhanced LCMV clearance is likely T cell-dependent, given the central role of T cells in LCMV immunity (Matloubian et al., 1994).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of LCMV immunity and correlation data

claim: The enhanced anti-viral response in the chronic absence of ZFP36 in KO mice is accompanied by spontaneous inflammation and autoimmunity that worsen with age.
source: Importantly, the enhanced anti-viral response in the chronic absence of ZFP36 in KO mice is accompanied by spontaneous inflammation and autoimmunity that worsen with age.
evidence: Based on known phenotype of Zfp36 KO mice

claim: Carefully titrated inhibition of ZFP36 might serve as a pharmacologic strategy in contexts where accelerated T cell response to challenge is desirable.
source: These data suggest carefully titrated inhibition of ZFP36 might serve as a pharmacologic strategy in contexts where accelerated T cell response to challenge is desirable.
evidence: Based on functional outcomes observed in Zfp36 KO mice

claim: ZFP36 HITS-CLIP identified many checkpoint inhibitor targets central to tumor immunity strategies.
source: ZPF36 HITS-CLIP identified many targets central to these strategies, including Cd274 (PD-L1), Pdcd1l2 (PD-L2), Icos, Cd27, Cd28, Ctla-4, Btla, and Lag3, suggesting a means for concerted regulation.
evidence: Based on HITS-CLIP target identification
